title: Big voltages and a sagging ST segment
presentingComplaint: Referred with blood pressure repeatedly above 170/100 mmHg despite two agents. He reports mild breathlessness on hills but no chest pain.
history: Hypertension diagnosed nine years ago, adherence variable
On amlodipine and ramipril; home readings consistently 165–180 systolic
Mild exertional breathlessness on hills over the past year
No chest pain, no orthopnoea, no syncope; non-smoker
symptoms: No chest pain at rest or on exertion
examinationFindings: Blood pressure 172/98 mmHg in both arms
Apex beat displaced laterally, forceful and sustained — a pressure-loaded apex
Fourth heart sound at the apex; no murmur
No signs of fluid overload; no radiofemoral delay

vitals.bedside: Comfortable at rest with a markedly raised blood pressure. The forceful sustained apex beat is the physical sign that matches the tracing.

ecg.pWaves: Broad and notched in lead II with a deep terminal negative component in V1 — left atrial abnormality
ecg.qrs: 0.10 s, narrow, but of high amplitude: tall R waves in I, aVL, V5 and V6 with deep S waves in V1 and V2
ecg.stSegment: Downsloping depression in I, aVL, V5 and V6, with reciprocal elevation over the deep S waves in V1 and V2
ecg.tWaves: Asymmetrically inverted in the lateral leads — a slow downstroke and a rapid return
keyFindings: Voltage criteria met: the sum of S in V1 and R in V5 exceeds 35 mm
Lateral strain pattern — downsloping ST depression with asymmetrical T wave inversion
Left atrial abnormality on the P wave, reflecting a stiff ventricle and raised filling pressure
A narrow QRS, which distinguishes this from bundle branch block as a cause of the repolarisation change

interpretation: Sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy and a lateral repolarisation (strain) pattern, together with left atrial abnormality. Findings are consistent with hypertensive heart disease; the ECG supports but does not establish the diagnosis, which is made by echocardiography.

auscultation.note: A low-pitched fourth heart sound just before S1, heard with the bell at the apex. It is the atrium contracting forcefully into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle — and it cannot exist in atrial fibrillation.
No ejection systolic murmur, which makes aortic stenosis unlikely as the cause of the hypertrophy.
No early diastolic murmur; aortic regurgitation would be another cause of left ventricular enlargement.

options.text: Sinus rhythm
options.feedback: Correct. The abnormality here is of voltage and repolarisation, not of rhythm.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation
options.feedback: The rhythm is regular and there are clear, if broad, P waves before every QRS.

options.text: Junctional rhythm
options.feedback: Upright, conducted P waves precede each QRS in lead II.

options.text: Accelerated idioventricular rhythm
options.feedback: The QRS is narrow at 0.10 s and follows a P wave.

questions.explanation: Naming the rhythm first, before commenting on morphology, keeps the systematic approach intact even when a striking abnormality catches the eye.

questions.prompt: Which measurement supports left ventricular hypertrophy here?

options.text: The sum of the S wave in V1 and the R wave in V5 exceeds 35 mm
options.feedback: Correct — the Sokolow–Lyon index. The Cornell criteria, using R in aVL plus S in V3, perform slightly better.

options.text: The QRS duration exceeds 0.12 s
options.feedback: That would indicate a conduction abnormality. The QRS here is 0.10 s.

options.text: The PR interval exceeds 0.20 s
options.feedback: The PR interval relates to atrioventricular conduction, not to ventricular mass.

options.text: The presence of Q waves in the inferior leads
options.feedback: Inferior Q waves suggest previous infarction, not hypertrophy.

questions.explanation: Voltage criteria are specific but insensitive. They over-call in thin young people and under-call in obesity, emphysema and pericardial effusion.

questions.prompt: How would you characterise the lateral ST and T wave changes?

options.text: Downsloping ST depression with asymmetrical T wave inversion — a strain pattern
options.feedback: Correct. The shape matters: strain T waves descend slowly and return steeply, whereas ischaemic inversion tends to be symmetrical.

options.text: Concave ST elevation in all leads
options.feedback: That is the pattern of acute pericarditis.

options.text: Symmetrical deep T wave inversion in V2–V4 with preserved R waves
options.feedback: That describes Wellens' pattern, which points to critical proximal left anterior descending stenosis and is a different, urgent finding.

options.text: Peaked, narrow-based T waves
options.feedback: That suggests hyperkalaemia.

questions.explanation: Describing T wave inversion as symmetrical or asymmetrical is a small habit that carries real diagnostic weight.

questions.prompt: Given the uncontrolled hypertension, the sustained apex beat and this tracing, what is the most likely interpretation?

options.text: Hypertensive left ventricular hypertrophy with a repolarisation strain pattern
options.feedback: Correct. The history, the pressure-loaded apex, the fourth heart sound and the ECG all point the same way.

options.text: Acute non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
options.feedback: The lateral ST depression is a real trap, but there is no chest pain, the changes are chronic in character and the voltages explain them. Serial troponin would settle any doubt.

options.text: Left bundle branch block
options.feedback: The QRS is 0.10 s — narrow. Left bundle branch block requires 0.12 s or more.

options.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
options.feedback: Possible on the ECG alone, and worth excluding by imaging — but nine years of poorly controlled hypertension is the simpler explanation.

questions.explanation: The same ECG in a young athlete with a normal blood pressure would raise very different possibilities. Context does most of the work.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate next step in this educational scenario?

options.text: Optimise blood pressure control and arrange echocardiography to confirm and quantify the hypertrophy
options.feedback: Correct. Imaging measures wall thickness and function directly, and blood pressure control can regress hypertrophy and improve outcomes.

options.text: Activate the primary percutaneous coronary intervention pathway
options.feedback: There is no ST elevation and no acute ischaemic presentation.

options.text: Reassure and repeat the ECG in five years
options.feedback: Electrocardiographic hypertrophy with a strain pattern is an independent marker of cardiovascular risk and warrants action now.

options.text: Stop his antihypertensives because the ECG explains the readings
options.feedback: The ECG is a consequence of the raised pressure, not an alternative to treating it.

questions.explanation: Educational scenario only. Hypertension management follows current guidelines and the assessment of the treating clinician.

explanation: Chronic pressure overload makes the left ventricle add sarcomeres in parallel, thickening its wall. More myocardium generates a larger vector directed leftward and posteriorly, so the leads that face the left ventricle record taller R waves and those on the right record deeper S waves — the basis of every voltage criterion. The repolarisation changes have a different cause: the subendocardium of a thick, high-pressure wall is relatively underperfused and repolarises out of sequence, producing downsloping ST depression and asymmetrical T inversion in the same lateral leads. A stiff ventricle also raises left atrial pressure, which is why the P wave is broad and notched and why there is an audible fourth heart sound. The tracing is supportive evidence: echocardiography measures the muscle.
learningObjectives: Apply the Sokolow–Lyon and Cornell voltage criteria correctly
Distinguish a strain pattern from ischaemic repolarisation change by T wave symmetry
Recognise left atrial abnormality and explain why it accompanies hypertrophy
State the limits of the ECG in diagnosing hypertrophy compared with imaging
clinicalContext: Voltage criteria are affected by body habitus, lung disease and lead placement. The ECG raises the possibility of hypertrophy; echocardiography or cardiac magnetic resonance confirms it and distinguishes hypertensive remodelling from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or infiltration.
